title: Indian Traditions in Depth
summary: Buddhism (Three Jewels, Three Marks, Five Skandhas, Four Noble Truths, Eightfold Path, sub-schools, Tripiṭaka); Jainism (ahiṃsā, jīva, kevalya jñāna, indriyas); Sufism (ṭarīqah, maqāmāt, nafs); Patañjali Yoga (eight limbs); Koshas; four states of consciousness; Bhagavad Gītā; Kuṇḍalinī and chakra yoga.

notes.t: Buddhism

Buddhism is a spiritual tradition founded by Siddhartha Gautama (the Buddha) in the 5th–4th century BCE. Its core teachings include the Three Jewels (Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha), the Three Marks of Existence (anicca — impermanence; dukkha — suffering; anattā — not-self), the Five Skandhas, the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path.

The Four Noble Truths: dukkha (suffering exists), samudaya (suffering arises from desire, attachment and craving), nirodha (liberation is possible by letting go of desires) and magga (the Eightfold Path leads to enlightenment and peace). The Eightfold Path — right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration — is organised into wisdom (prajñā), ethical conduct (śīla) and mental discipline (samādhi).

The Five Skandhas (pañca skandha) are the five aggregates that make up a person's experience of reality: rūpa (form), vedanā (sensation/feeling), saññā (perception), saṅkhāra (mental formations) and viññāṇa (consciousness). Buddhism teaches anattā (no-self) — what we call the self is a temporary collection of these aggregates.

Major sub-schools: Theravāda ('The School of the Elders,' also called Hīnayāna), Mahāyāna ('The Great Vehicle') and Vajrayāna ('The Diamond Vehicle,' Tibetan). The sacred canon is the Tripiṭaka (Three Baskets) — Sutta Piṭaka, Vinaya Piṭaka and Abhidhamma Piṭaka.
Jainism

Jainism originated around the 6th century BCE, with Lord Mahāvīra as its 24th and last Tīrthaṅkara. Jain monks and followers practise strict non-violence (ahiṃsā), truth, celibacy and non-possessiveness.

Jīva (living being) — every living being is a soul or consciousness that is alive and aware, and is an active agent (not passive). Each jīva inherently possesses jñāna (knowledge), but karmic impurities cloud it; when overcome, the jīva becomes a Jina — one who has conquered ignorance and reached kevalya jñāna (absolute knowledge). Living beings are classified by the number of indriyas (senses) they possess — gyanendriya (physical sense organs) and bhavendriya (psychic sense organs).
Sufism

Sufism is the mystical dimension of Islam. Its path (ṭarīqah) proceeds through spiritual stations (maqāmāt). The layers are sharīʿah (foundational stage — Islamic law and ethical conduct), ṭarīqah (mystical path, guided by a sheikh/pir), maʿrifah (deep inner realisation) and ḥaqīqah (final stage — divine knowledge and unity with God).

Levels of the self (nafs): the commanding self (nafs al-ammāra — dominated by base desires), the blaming self (nafs al-lawwāma — recognises moral shortcomings), the inspired self, the secure self, the gratified self and the complete self (unity with divine consciousness).
Patañjali Yoga and the Eight Limbs

Sāṅkhya philosophy is the basis for Patañjali's Yoga Sūtra. Patañjali defined yoga as citta-vṛtti-nirodha — the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind. The goal is samādhi (absorption/enlightenment). Yoga has eight limbs (aṣṭāṅga): yama (moral restraints), niyama (observances), āsana (posture), prāṇāyāma (breath control), pratyāhāra (withdrawal of senses), dhāraṇā (concentration), dhyāna (meditation) and samādhi (absorption).
Koshas and States of Consciousness

The koshas (sheaths), from the Taittirīya Upanishad, describe layers of the self: annamaya (food body — basic needs such as food, water, sleep), prāṇamaya (breath body — air/breathing), manomaya (mental body — thoughts, emotions, feelings, desires, memories), vijñānamaya (intelligence body — buddhi, reasoning, decision-making) and ānandamaya (bliss body — supreme state of bliss; self-absorption/samādhi).

Advait Vedānta describes four states of consciousness (from the Māṇḍūkya Upanishad): jāgrat (wakeful state), svapna (dream state), prajña (superconsciousness/transcendental state) and turīya (highest state — the essential nature of ātman is experienced).
Bhagavad Gītā

The Bhagavad Gītā offers wisdom on self-awareness, duty and inner balance across its 18 chapters (e.g., Karma Yoga — action, Bhakti Yoga — devotion, Jñāna Yoga — knowledge, Dhyāna Yoga — meditation). The path to self-realisation combines abhyāsa (practice), jñāna (knowledge), dhyāna (meditation), tyāga (renunciation) and śānti (peace).
Kuṇḍalinī and Chakra Yoga

Kuṇḍalinī yoga centres on awakening the kuṇḍalinī energy — often symbolised as a serpent coiled at the root chakra at the base of the spine — guided upward through the chakras until it reaches the crown chakra. Chakra yoga works with seven chakras: mūlādhāra (root), svādhiṣṭhāna (sacral), maṇipūra (solar plexus), anāhata (heart), viśuddha (throat), ājña (third eye) and sahasrāra (crown).
Examination connection

Buddhism's Three Marks (anicca, dukkha, anattā), Five Skandhas, Four Noble Truths and Eightfold Path recur in matching questions. Patañjali's eight limbs and the nine rasas are frequently examined in Indian psychology questions.
